title: Prethermal ripplons in quenched binary Bose-Einstein condensates
authors: Yanda Geng, Stephen Eckel, Gretchen K. Campbell, Ian B. Spielman
abstract: Prethermal states--long-lived quasi-equilibrium configurations--occur in a wide range of physical systems that exhibit fast dephasing or reconfiguration followed by slow relaxation towards thermal equilibrium. We experimentally studied the 1D interface between immiscible 2D Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs); following a quench, the interfacial capillary waves (ripplons) quickly relaxed into a long-lived prethermal state characterized by a persistent non-equipartition of energy, evoking the classic Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou problem. We directly measured the interface's height profile as it evolved in time, identified the contribution of individual ripplon modes, and find that, though their individual amplitudes are thermally distributed, they are not in thermal equilibrium--high-momentum modes rapidly equilibrated with the bulk phonon modes of the 2D BEC, while lower momentum modes remained at elevated temperatures, forming a long-lived prethermal configuration for the whole system. We attribute this to kinematic isolation: the absence of energy- and momentum-conserving relaxation processes in our system at ultracold temperature.
summary: This work experimentally demonstrates prethermalization in the ripplons at the interface of two immiscible Bose-Einstein condensates. The authors show that while high-momentum modes rapidly thermalize with the bulk, low-momentum modes remain trapped at elevated temperatures. This slow relaxation is attributed to kinematic isolation, providing a clear realization of non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum gases.
main_problem: The paper investigates how far-from-equilibrium quantum systems, specifically interfacial waves in BECs, approach thermal equilibrium, focusing on the phenomenon of prethermalization.
main_result: Low-momentum ripplon modes exhibit persistent, elevated temperatures relative to the bulk phonon bath, forming a long-lived prethermal state due to kinematic isolation.
method: The study combines theoretical modeling (Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism, Hamiltonian derivation) with experimental measurements of time-evolving interface height profiles and mode temperatures.
model_or_system: The system is a 1D interface between immiscible 2D Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). The dynamics are modeled by interfacial capillary waves (ripplons) coupled to the bulk phonon modes.
key_observables: Interface height profile $h(x)$, Power Spectral Density $\langle|h_k|^2angle$, and the effective temperature $T_k$ of individual ripplon modes.
important_parameters: Interfacial tension ($\sigma$), bulk temperature ($T_{	ext{bulk}}$), and the wave number $k$.
main_assumptions: The slow relaxation of low-momentum modes is attributed to kinematic isolation, meaning the absence of energy- and momentum-conserving relaxation processes coupling them to the bulk bath.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relaxation process from initial quench to prethermal state, comparing measured power spectra to equilibrium predictions, and showing mode temperatures decaying with wave number and time.
paper_structure: The paper develops the Hamiltonian for the ripplon field, analyzes the dispersion relation, and then presents experimental evidence showing that high-$k$ modes thermalize quickly while low-$k$ modes remain trapped in a non-equilibrium, prethermal state.
why_interesting: It provides a clean, experimentally accessible platform (BEC interfaces) to study fundamental non-equilibrium statistical mechanics concepts like prethermalization and energy partitioning in quantum many-body systems.
